newsitem.title: UK: British party launches anti-EU election crusade.
newsitem.headline: British party launches anti-EU election crusade.

text.p: An anti-European fringe party set out its stall on Monday for Britain's May 1 election, with its leader saying an appeal to voters for a divorce between London and Brussels might just win it a seat or two in parliament.
Alan Sked, who heads the UK Independence Party, pulled no punches in his attack on the European Union.

"It is the most bizarre set of undemocratic, unaccountable, incompetent, financially-profligate institutions that the world has ever seen," he told reporters at the launch of the UKIP's first general election manifesto.
"The only way is out," the manifesto said. "The...policy of withdrawal is the only viable option."
The UKIP will field candidates in less than a third of the 659 seats being contested at the election.
Political observers say it has no chance of winning even a single seat, although it may make it even more difficult for the ruling Conservatives to retain power by taking votes from them.

But Sked maintains the economic bonus from withdrawal from the EU is so dazzling that if only the 80 percent of electors who oppose British membership get the message, his party could sweep to success in a few localities.
"We're hoping we might win two or three seats. I think it's possible," Sked said.
Both the ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party are committed to staying in the EU, although both are cautious about joining a single currency.
The UKIP says Britain could slash unemployment and be 20 billion pounds ($32 billion) a year better off within five years if it replaced EU membership with a free trade agreement with Europe.
"I don't see these forecasts as optimistic. I think they're rather cautious," Sked said.

The UKIP's main rival on the anti-EU platform is the Referendum Party, founded and financed by billionaire Anglo-French entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith. He aims to force a plebiscite on Britain's ties with Europe, saying the views of the majority of the country's voters are being ignored.
Sked says the UKIP, with around 16,000 members in Britain, has a far wider range of policies and a broader support base than the Referendum Party,

He said his party would fight on whatever its poll results. "This is the beginning on an epic struggle," he said. "It may take 10 years, but I expect Britain will get out of the EU." ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
